newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MOF takes steps to further deregulate banks.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF takes steps to further deregulate banks.

text.p: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) announced on Monday measures to further deregulate the banking industry in a bid to accelerate the "Big Bang" reform of Japan's financial system.
The steps will ease rules which have restricted ordinary banks such as city banks from raising long-term funds and also allow them more freedom in opening new branches.
The measures will also deregulate rules concerning investment trusts.
The main points of the steps are as follows:
1. Ordinary banks will be allowed to issue subordinated bonds. The measure will take effect from June 30.
2. The present upper limit of three years imposed on the period of floating rate term deposits will be abolished. The measure will take effect from April 1998.
3. Rules limiting the issuance of certificates of deposit (CDs) to over two weeks and within five years will be abolished as of April 1998.
4. Issues of euroyen bonds and foreign currency-denominated bonds by ordinary banks will be allowed sometime within the second half of fiscal 1999/2000.
5. Rules which limit business between trust banking subsidiaries and their parent banks will be wholly or partially abolished.
6. Regional financial institutions will be able to handle trust fund business such as real estate mangement trust and public trust funds from October 1.
7. Measures to ease rules on setting up branch offices and business hours will be taken within July.
8. Rules limiting those permitted to make subordinated loans to banks will be eased in July. Currently, such lenders are limited to insurance firms and non-banks.
9. Rules followed by banks in paying dividends and boosting capital will be scrapped during July.
